paragraphs.source_en: I had long heard that among low-class students there were indeed savages who ate cats, but I had never dreamed that Mr. Tatara himself, who had usually shown me so much kindness, was one of those barbarians. Moreover, he was no longer a student; though it was not long since he graduated, he was after all a respectable Bachelor of Laws and an employee of the Mitsui Company. My astonishment was therefore no ordinary thing. The maxim, “When you see a man, take him for a thief,” had already been proved by the conduct of Kangetsu the Second; but that “when you see a man, take him for a cat-eater” was a truth I had never imagined until Mr. Tatara kindly brought it home to me. The longer one lives in the world, the more one learns; and though knowledge is a pleasant thing, danger increases day by day, and day by day one can less afford to be careless. To become cunning, to become base, to put on a double-faced suit of protective clothing: all these are consequences of knowing too much. It is the sin of growing old. Perhaps that is why there are so few good people among the old. For a cat such as myself, it may be wiser, before I grow old, to attain Buddhahood at once in Mr. Tatara’s cat sukiyaki pot together with the onions. As I crouched in a corner, the more I thought the more frightened I became; just then my master, who had quarreled with his wife a moment before and retired in anger to the study, heard Mr. Tatara’s voice and came lumbering into the sitting room.
